title: Electrostatics
standard_text: Two kinds of charge; charging by friction; the principle of conservation of charge; charge sharing between identical conductors, Q = (Q₁ + Q₂)/2; quantisation of charge, Q = nqₑ; polarisation of insulators. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 10, Physics: Electrostatics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): positive and negative charge, charging by friction, conservation of charge, charge sharing and quantisation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
key_sub: Charge is conserved and comes in multiples of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
body_html:
How to think about it

Objects become charged by gaining or losing electrons: an object that gains electrons becomes negative, one that loses electrons becomes positive. Charge cannot be created or destroyed; it is only transferred.

When two identical conductors touch, they share the total charge equally: Q = (Q₁ + Q₂)/2. Charge is quantised: Q = n × 1,6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, where n is the number of electrons. A charged object attracts a neutral insulator by polarising it.

Example

+6 nC and −2 nC identical spheres touch. Charge on each?

(6 + (−2))/2

Answer: +2 nC

Example

A rod loses 5 × 10¹⁰ electrons. Its charge?

Q = ne

Answer: +8 × 10⁻⁹ C

Common mistakes

  • Thinking positive charges (protons) move when objects are rubbed.
  • Adding the charges without halving them.
  • Thinking a neutral object has no charges at all.

items.q: Is salt water an electrical conductor or an insulator?
c: neither: it can never be charged
items.e: Conductors have charges (such as free electrons) that can move; insulators hold charges in place, so they can be charged by rubbing.

items.q: In a demo, two pith balls carry charges that are positive and positive. What happens?

items.q: A negatively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. What happens to the electrons in the sphere?
c: They are repelled to the far side of the sphere.
They are attracted to the near side.
items.e: In charging by induction, a nearby charged object pushes or pulls electrons; earthing lets electrons flow; the sphere ends with the opposite charge to the rod.

items.q: Clothes stick together after a dryer cycle. Which explanation is best?

Protons moved from one object to the other.
Electrons moved from the glass to the silk.
items.e: Only electrons move between objects.
